sources.title: "Thoughts and Prayers" in Greek Tragedy

discussion.body: The phrase fails because it has become routine, not because prayer is inherently empty. Aeschylus gives the words weight by making speech itself risky.
“Dangerously performative” sounds like a warning about speech in general; the play’s energy is in debate about petition as a way to heal the city, which is closer to deliberation than incantation.

items.title: Aeschylus Made Prayer a Dangerous Performance
items.body:
“Thoughts and prayers” has lost its consolatory force: the phrase is meant to signal authentic care, but it has become so conventional that it is hard to imagine what the prayers contain or what effect they are supposed to have.

In Aeschylus’s Seven Against Thebes, Eva Stehl describes a world in which “speaking is dangerously performative.” The play’s drama is contained not in violent or spectacular set pieces but in urgent dialogue between the chorus and Eteokles about how best to heal the city through divine petition.

sources.title: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep your house warmer for longer

discussion.body: A fireplace is a fine money-saver for people who already have one. For everyone else, it is less a tip than a reminder that the cheapest heating is the heating you already own.
The sharper warning is Seymour’s: skipping the heating altogether is not a saving if it risks health problems or frozen pipes.

items.title: A Fireplace Can Be Cheaper Than Heating the Whole House
items.body:
The BBC reports that rising energy prices are making heating homes more expensive. The British Heart Foundation recommends wearing lots of thin layers rather than one thick layer to trap heat.

If you have a fireplace, lighting a fire to warm the room you are in can be cheaper than turning on central heating for the whole house. But Seymour says she would not recommend not having the heating on at all, citing health issues and how pipes can freeze over.

sources.title: France prepares for day of protest a week after nationwide riots

discussion.body: A rule that only recognised unions may demonstrate is a curious kind of permission: it does not ban protest so much as decide which protest gets to count as legitimate.

The organisers hardly seem deterred: hundreds of large and small demonstrations are planned across France. With cities setting different rules, the result looks less like a clean ban than a patchwork.

items.title: France's Saturday Protests Come With 70,000 Police and a Legal Filter
items.body:
France is on high alert ahead of Saturday's nationwide protests, a week after what the BBC calls some of the country's worst unrest in decades.

The interior ministry says it will deploy 70,000 police officers, after opposition parties accused the government of failing to foresee the scale of the unrest on 17 October.

Macron decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by recognised trade unions would be permitted on Saturday; Lyon, Nice and Montpellier have gone further by announcing blanket bans on gatherings.

sources.title: Why does every film and TV series seem to have the same plot?

discussion.body: A philosophy flip is a strange thing to schedule, but the formula does it: the old self stops working at the low point, and then the protagonist goes home to the same place as someone different.
That return is also the conservative part: the hero changes, while the place is declared the same. In cinema especially, that is a comforting ritual—and a convenient one.

items.title: The Movie Formula's Quietest Beat: Home, Transformed
items.body:
Aeon's essay starts from a provocation: we live in an era of apparently unprecedented choice, yet almost every film and TV series—along with many plays and novels—has exactly the same plot.

At the low point, the protagonist realises their old mode of being is redundant, but the new one is too daunting. The essay says the important thing is that their life philosophy has been turned upside down.

Then comes the return home: everything is the same, but everything is also completely transformed. The formula, the essay notes, is particularly repetitive in cinema.

sources.title: Knicks sent employees fake offer of championship rings in phishing test: Report

discussion.body: Corporate phishing tests are common, and a good one often looks like it came from inside the company—right down to a telltale flaw.
Common, sure, but this lure is memorable: it promises a reward and asks for a choice between two designs.

items.title: A Knicks phishing test dangled championship rings; clickers got a mandatory cybersecurity class
items.body:
The New York Knicks organization sent employees a phishing email that promised free championship rings, as a test of whether staff could spot a scam, The New York Times reported. The message, sent in late September, began “Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here,” and told employees to click a link to choose between two ring designs.

Madison Square Garden employees who took the bait were forced to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class, according to the report, which cited team sources; the class was meant to help address owner James Dolan’s growing cybersecurity concerns.

sources.title: Archimedes Rediscovered: Technology and Ancient History

discussion.body: A prayer book is a strange hiding place for a mathematician, but it is also a very human one: the Archimedes text sits beneath later prayers, one century’s devotional reading covering another’s.

The human chain around the prayer book matters more than the irony: a buyer paid $2 million and donated the manuscript to the Walters Art Museum, where Wilson could study it. The UV lamps get the drama; the donor gets the assist.

The lamps revealed the text; Wilson still had to read it closely. In the 2004 report, he caught an error in Heiberg’s translation of a single word after a lengthy examination of one passage, refining its meaning.

items.title: A prayer book hid lost Archimedes texts. UV lamps and digital photography helped reveal them
items.body:
In 1907, Johan Ludvig Heiberg found something unexpected in a Byzantine prayer book: beneath the prayers, in faded lettering, he recognized the words of Archimedes. The book held several lost texts by the ancient Greek mathematician, erased sometime in the 13th century.

A buyer paid $2 million for the artifact and donated it to the Walters Art Museum, where classicists including Nigel Wilson finally got the opportunity to study the manuscript. In a 2004 progress report, Wilson described how technologies such as UV lamps and digital photography allowed researchers to reveal and share lost ancient works. The manuscript contained lost works by Archimedes including Method, On Floating Bodies, and parts of Stomachion.

sources.title: Israel orders closure of West Bank after soldiers kill 2 men behind an alleged attack

discussion.body: The army's account names the weapons and says it foiled a terror attack, but leaves the target of the alleged attack unexplained.
Netanyahu's response went further on blame than on detail: he convened an emergency Security Cabinet meeting and accused Hamas of planning a major attack, without elaborating on what it entailed.

items.title: Two men killed near Hebron as Israeli voters weigh Netanyahu's next term
items.body:
Israeli soldiers shot and killed two men who the military said had launched an attack near the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning. The army said it prevented a “terror attack against Israeli civilians” and that the gunmen carried an M16 rifle and a handgun.

At least five people were injured, including some critically. The shooting comes as Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Netanyahu yet another term as prime minister.

sources.title: Calcidius the Latin Plato

discussion.body: The oddity is that obscurity and centrality are not opposites here: the same man could be the West's main Plato for eight centuries and a name almost nobody knows now.
But the reverence was never simple. A figure who draws either extravagant praise or excessive scorn is hard to treat as a calm authority.

items.title: For eight centuries, the West met Plato through a translator barely anyone has heard of now
items.body:
Calcidius translated the first half of Plato's Timaeus into Latin and wrote a very detailed commentary on its technical aspects. These days, barely anyone has heard of him, let alone read his work.

For eight centuries, he was the main source of knowledge about Plato in the western world, revered as a Latin Plato.

His reputation has always been polarizing: he drew either extravagant praise or excessive scorn. Gercke, then in his twenties and just starting as a language instructor at the Luisengymnasium in Berlin, made a pronouncement whose harshness may owe something to youth and a desire to appear as a linguistic connoisseur.

sources.title: Inquiry looking into man's death in Edmonton ER hears about too many patients, not enough beds or doctors

discussion.body: The 20 to 30 per cent figure is the one to sit with: a hospital can be full while the missing piece is accommodation or a service outside it.
That doesn't turn “more doctors won't solve it” into “staffing doesn't matter.” The claim is about chronic overcrowding, not every problem a ward can have.

items.title: An Edmonton Fatality Inquiry Hears That More Doctors Won't Fix the Overcrowding
items.body:
At a fatality inquiry into a man's death in the Grey Nuns emergency department, a physician testified that hiring more doctors would not solve the Edmonton hospital's chronic overcrowding. He described an actual physical limit to what care the facility can provide.

The inquiry heard that overcrowding also happens when patients who no longer need hospital care cannot be discharged because the services or accommodation they need are not available.

The physician estimated that 20 to 30 per cent of beds are occupied by such patients at any given time.

sources.title: Danny Boyle on his tabloid chronicle Ink: “The attention economy, clickbait, the dopamine economy – this is its hatching point”

discussion.body: The typewriter correction is the funniest kind of pedantry: wrong on set, right in the memory. The accent is what actually unlocks the recollection.
The accent is the richer detail because it carries class: a northern accent with refinement, an attempt to assimilate into the posh world.

items.title: Ink's Typewriters Were Wrong; the Accent Was Right
items.body:
Danny Boyle's Ink, his 15th feature, mirrors the excitement of the Sun's rise while exposing the morally dubious decisions Lamb's team made to achieve its popularity.

The people who overheard a scene were typical journalists: their verdict was that all the typewriters were wrong. They would have been Olivetti 2s in 1969; the film had Olivetti 3s, the only ones available.

The accent was the trigger: the journalists recognized the performance.

sources.title: Intel gets waiver after worries fuzzy US ban on foreign-made robots may hit fabs

discussion.body: A waiver is a useful admission that a rule's edge cases are blurry. If Intel, of all companies, can't tell whether its chip-fab robots are covered, the ban's scope is doing too much work in the dark.
Or the waiver is exactly how a cautious regulator should handle a blurry line: grant a one-year exception and let the fabs keep running.

items.title: Intel Got a One-Year Waiver From a Robot Ban It Couldn't Parse
items.body:
Intel was confused enough by the US government ban on foreign-made robots that it requested and received a waiver “out of an abundance of caution.”

The FCC's October 22 order lets Intel keep using the foreign-made robots in US semiconductor manufacturing facilities for one year.

Intel's website describes the robots as automated guided vehicles that run on tracks or predefined paths, often with operator oversight. They help move materials around warehouses and factory floors.

sources.title: Severe flooding hits Four Corners region, more expected through the weekend

discussion.body: The riverfront line is the sharpest detail: the same feature that makes these communities lovely is what puts homes in the path of brown water.
But the scale is regional, not just one riverfront: rare heavy rain began Wednesday across four states, and since then floodwaters have closed roads and forced evacuations.

items.title: A Blue Sky Over San Juan County While Brown Water Floods Homes
items.body:
On Friday afternoon, Devin Neeley looked out a window in San Juan County, N.M., and saw light, puffy clouds and a blue sky. Meanwhile, brown rainwaters were flooding homes in low-lying parts of the county and forcing sewage into the San Juan River. Neeley said these are communities with beautiful riverfront places to live, which is unfortunately a problem today.

Rare, heavy rainfall began hitting the Four Corners region—New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona—on Wednesday. Since then, severe brown floodwaters have led to road closures, mandatory evacuations and emergency declarations across the four states. A southern Utah city issued an emergency declaration on Thursday after flooding damaged more than 100 homes and RVs.

sources.title: NASA’s Swift Mission Ends, Leaves Behind Scientific Bonanza

discussion.body: Eleven X-ray photons sounds like a rounding error, but they came from a 0.03-second burst and were enough to make it the first short gamma-ray burst with a detected afterglow.

The harder problem was not collecting photons but finding the burst fast enough; short bursts peak in under two seconds, and before Swift it was impossible to locate them precisely enough to observe afterglows.

items.title: NASA's Swift Turned Fast Enough to Catch a 0.03-Second Gamma-Ray Burst
items.body:
NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has ended its science mission. It is orbiting less than 171 miles above Earth, where greater atmospheric drag prevents its telescopes from steadily gazing at their targets.

Short gamma-ray bursts reach peak brightness in less than two seconds. Until Swift, it had been impossible to locate these bursts rapidly and precisely enough to observe their afterglows. In May 2005, Swift achieved that with GRB 050509B, which lasted just 0.03 seconds. Swift turned to the burst fast enough to detect 11 X-ray photons, making this the first short burst with a detected afterglow.

sources.title: Seeking to help Collins in Maine, Trump exempts some Canadian imports from his 50% tariffs

discussion.body: Plywood sheets and packing crates are a wonderfully concrete unit of trade politics: not a doctrine, just a short list of things Maine businesses buy and a senator in a tight race can ask to have excused.

Cheaper inputs are genuine relief for whoever buys them, but if importers absorb the cost rather than pass it on, the win arrives as thinner margins rather than lower prices on the shelf — which is a harder thing to campaign on.

items.title: Trump Trims Canadian Tariffs to Help Collins in Maine. Importers Still Pay.
items.body:
President Donald Trump, seeking to help Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a tough reelection battle in Maine, is exempting some imports — plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery among them — from the 50% tariffs he put on $20 billion worth of Canadian products over the summer, the Associated Press reports. The changes take effect Oct. 30.

The money does not come from Canada: the president has claimed that foreign countries pay his tariffs, but U.S. importers do. Those importers then face a choice between passing the higher cost to customers and absorbing it, which is the price the exemption actually changes.

sources.title: Was Homer’s Ithaca an Island?

discussion.body: What I like is the refusal to let a place-name settle an argument. Most people supposed Ithaki was Ithaca, and that kind of inherited consensus is exactly the kind that rarely gets tested.
Fair, but a theory that has to explain away a 6km land bridge is carrying weight the map doesn't show. A peninsula is not a rounding error, and the burden of proof should sit with the clever reading.

items.title: The Case That Odysseus's Ithaca Is a Peninsula Called Paliki
items.body:
An essay in Antigone on where Homer's Ithaca actually lay starts from Odysseus's own description of his homeland, which it reads as putting Ithaca west of three islands: Doulichion, Same and Zacynthos.

The essay credits Robert Bittlestone with the conclusion that Ithaca cannot be the modern island of Ithaki, as most people have supposed. His alternative is that Ithaca is the western peninsula of Cephalonia, today called Paliki after its ancient capital city Paleis.

The obstacle is right there on the map. Paliki is not an island; it is a peninsula joined to the main body of Cephalonia by a narrow land bridge 6km long and 2km wide, centred on the Thinia Valley. So the identification works only if a poem's directions are allowed to outrank the coastline we can see.

sources.title: 'I'm glad that he's gone': Winnipeg Jets fans say messy exit tarnishes Hellebuyck's legacy

discussion.body: The trade looks less like a haul than a salvage operation. Marek said the Jets were in no position to win it: goalies don't go for big prices, and a distressed asset everyone knows wants out leaves no leverage.
Fans may not care about the ledger. Gord Walters said he was glad Hellebuyck was gone, and that while he was a good goalie, it was time for a change.

items.title: The Jets' Return for a Three-Time Vezina Winner: Four Players and Two Picks
items.body:
Connor Hellebuyck asked for a trade at the end of last season, with five years still left on a seven-year contract. He is a three-time Vezina Trophy winner and the 2025 league MVP. He has been traded to New Jersey following a drawn-out spat with the team that drafted him in 2012.

In exchange, the Jets acquired forwards Dawson Mercer, Alexander Command and Nick Bjugstad, and goalie Nico Daws. They also got New Jersey's second-round pick in the 2029 NHL draft and a seventh-round pick in 2027.

sources.title: ‘Overnight, everything was dead’: the Teesside fisherman turned activist dubbed the Mr Bates of the seas

discussion.body: The official explanations are part of the story: after carrying out their own tests, the authorities denied a causal link, blaming an algae bloom and later a novel pathogen. People who live and work around the Tees estuary disagreed.
An absence of an official cause is not the same as no cause. Finlay is right that she can't offer an easy answer, but a film can honor uncertainty without letting it harden into the conclusion.

items.title: A Mass Crustacean Die-Off Documentary Starts With 'No Official Cause'
items.body:
On 25 September 2021, thousands of dead and dying crustaceans washed up on beaches in Yorkshire and the north-east of England. Jeanie Finlay's documentary All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea is not setting out to find what killed the crabs and lobsters.

Finlay says she can't offer an easy answer to what happened: there isn't an official cause. What she can do, she says, is show the audience what that feels like.

sources.title: RS-25 Engine Tests at NASA Stennis

discussion.body: The useful part is that this is a developmental engine: NASA gets performance and reliability data from hardware that will not be used in flight.

That is the glass-half-full reading. The flight configuration is still four engines producing up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust, and the test engine will not be used in flight; the data is the product, not a flight qualification.

items.title: NASA ran an RS-25 for a full launch burn at 111% power
items.body:
Teams at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, hot-fired RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21, 2026. The burn lasted almost 500 seconds—the same duration the engines fire during an SLS launch—at 111% power.

This developmental engine will not fly, but NASA says the test gives the agency and prime contractor L3Harris Technologies data to improve engine performance and reliability. For each Artemis mission, four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket.

sources.title: 10 great East African films

discussion.body: The Cannes first is the headline, but the more revealing part is what the selection points to: a longstanding lack of international recognition and circulation for cinema from East Africa and the wider continent. One breakthrough film does not undo that.

The festival first is less interesting than the form. Setting the story inside a gacaca makes the courtroom itself the dramatic machinery, putting the film in the company of Bamako and Joshua Oppenheimer’s interrogations of life alongside, and forgiveness of, those responsible for atrocities.

items.title: The first film by a Rwandan filmmaker in Cannes’ official selection looks inside a gacaca court
items.body:
Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Ben’Imana opens this year’s Film Africa with an intergenerational reckoning with the aftermath of Rwanda’s 1994 Tutsi genocide.

The film puts viewers inside a gacaca, an open-air court rooted in indigenous judicial traditions and adapted to facilitate justice and reconciliation after the genocide.

It won the Caméra d’Or at Cannes and is the first film directed by a Rwandan filmmaker to be included in the festival’s official selection.

sources.title: Why Olivia Colman Didn’t Get Splinters From Getting Intimate With Alexander Skarsgård’s ‘Wicker’ Costume

discussion.body: The interesting constraint is the request itself: make it practically. The result was a laser-sintered print, so “practical” here means a fabricated physical weave, not necessarily a traditional one.
Fair, but thermoplastic elastomer and laser-fused powder are about as un-pastoral as a basket weave gets. The engineering is impressive; the premise remains funny.

items.title: Wicker’s Intricate Basket Weave Was Printed From Fused Powder
items.body:
For “Wicker,” now in theaters, the writers and directors told Weta Workshop’s Joe Dunckley and Sarah Rubano that they wanted to make it practically, Dunckley says.

The intricate basket weave was created using a relatively new powder-bed laser-sintered printing process. Dunckley explains that a laser is fired into a volume of thermoplastic elastomer powder and fuses it at the focal point, allowing intricate weave and complex geometry to be built.
